deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is page 6 (folio 88) of German lecture notes or excerpts on ancient Greek history, specifically the opening of the Peloponnesian War. The neighbouring pages continue the same narrative: Mytilene, Corcyra, Brasidas, Amphipolis, the Peace of Nicias in 421. The style (a dated narrative with a running margin of keywords and dates) is typical of Göttingen history lectures of the period, for example in the manner of Heeren. The hand and content do not obviously belong to Gauss's mathematical papers, so authorship or provenance (Gauss's own notes, or a copied lecture Nachschrift) is uncertain.

Content, step by step:
(1) Continuing the list from the previous page of Athens' allies: Greek cities (probably in Thrace and/or Asia Minor), plus several allies on the mainland. A cross-reference '+' points to the margin: Naupactus, Plataeae and all of Acarnania.
(2) Sparta's allies: the whole Peloponnese except Argos and Achaea, most states of Greece proper, and the island of Leucas.
(3) Margin note: the war has its own historian, Thucydides, who himself held a command on the Athenian side.
(4) Pericles, who had advised war, held the command at first. The Athenians were to stay on the defensive. 60,000 Peloponnesians invaded Attica, while Athens had barely 30,000 men. Pericles drew the rural population into the city; the countryside was ravaged. These were at first mere raids. The Athenian fleet in turn ravaged Laconia.
(5) Diplomacy: Sparta sought to win Persia to its side; Athens allied with the kings of Thrace (Sitalces) and Macedon (Perdiccas).
(6) Margin: Pericles died in 429 of the plague. His death was an irreplaceable loss. While he lived, the harmful effects of democracy had not appeared; now unworthy men came forward, and Cleon, a tanner, came to the helm.
(7) Cleon took the small island of Sphacteria (425), putting the Peloponnesians in the greatest danger. In the first years the war was waged without a fixed plan.
(8) '427 griffen die Athener ...' continues on the next page with Mytilene on Lesbos.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations. The only numbers are dates and army sizes.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.
Minor historical simplification: the 60,000 figure for the invading Peloponnesian army comes from Plutarch (Pericles 33) and is not given by Thucydides; modern historians consider it exaggerated.
'kaum 30000 Mann' for Athens roughly matches Thucydides II.13: 13,000 field hoplites, 16,000 garrison troops, plus cavalry and archers, so this is acceptable.
The order of events is compressed: Sphacteria (425) is narrated before the '427' entry, so the narrative is not strictly chronological.

results.what: Narrative notes on the opening phase of the Peloponnesian War (alliances, Pericles' defensive strategy, Pericles' death in 429, Cleon, Sphacteria)
results.modern_name: Standard ancient history (Thucydides, Books I–IV; Plutarch, Pericles)
results.usually_credited_to: Thucydides; Plutarch; standard 18th/19th-century university history lectures (e.g. Heeren at Göttingen)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical: routine history lecture notes on the Peloponnesian War. Even if written by Gauss, it would only document an interest in classical history, which is already well known (he had classical training and studied at Göttingen). There is nothing here of mathematical significance.

checkable.asserts: The war lasting from 431 to 404 BC is the '27-year war' named on the previous page.
Pericles died (429 BC) in the third campaigning year, two years after the outbreak (431 BC).
The invading Peloponnesian force as stated outnumbered the Athenian force two to one.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'Rechte[?] an Bündner[?] erhielten[?]' is almost certainly 'Städte in [Thracien / Asien?] ...'. It continues 'die griechischen' from the previous page, i.e. 'die griechischen Städte in ...'.
'mehrere Verbündete außer dem Festlande +' should probably read 'auf dem Festlande +'. The marginal referent (Naupactus, Plataeae, Akarnanien) consists of mainland allies.
'Der athenienische Rath schob[?] anfangs Perikles das Commando' probably reads something like 'Bei den Atheniensern hatte/führte anfangs Perikles das Commando'.

'Dann aber waren die Athenienser selbst[?] sich vertheidigend aufs[?]. [?] machte[?] ein 60000 Mann Spartaner einfallen in Attika[?] und[?]' probably reads 'Denn ... die Athenienser sollten sich vertheidigungsweise verhalten. 60000 Mann Spartaner rückten in Attika ein; die Athener hatten kaum 30000 Mann.'
'darauf bedacht, Persien[?] für ihre Interesse zu ziehen': 'Persien' looks correct; it is probably 'in ihr Interesse zu ziehen'.
'der Peloponnes ertrug[?] die größte Gefahr[?]' is uncertain; the sense is that the Peloponnesians were thereby put in the greatest danger.
Margin: 'Er war bei dem Ath.[?] feldzug[?] mit Anführer' likely reads 'Er war bei dem Athenischen Heer mit Anführer'.
Margin: 'Plataeae' and 'Akarnanien' are written as 'Plataeae' and 'Acarnanien/Akarnanien'. The '+' after Achaja in the main text is a separate cross-mark.
